title: Birbal's Entry to Akbar's Court
full_text:
Long before he was known throughout Hindustan as Raja Birbal, a clever young scholar named Mahesh Das lived in a modest village. One afternoon while hunting in the dense forest near Agra, Emperor Akbar became separated from his royal retinue. Thirsty, exhausted, and hopelessly lost at a junction of three dusty roads, the monarch encountered young Mahesh Das carrying a bundle of firewood.

Akbar called out, 'Young man, which of these roads goes to Agra?'

Mahesh Das smiled gently and replied, 'Sire, roads do not walk! People walk, but roads stay exactly where they are. If you follow the path on the right, you shall reach the red walls of Agra.'

Amused by the youth's quick wit, the Emperor revealed his identity, gave Mahesh Das his signet ring, and invited him to the imperial palace. Months later, Mahesh Das traveled to Agra to claim the Emperor's favor. However, the palace gatekeeper was notoriously corrupt. Seeing the royal ring, the greedy guard sneered, 'I will let you enter only if you swear to give me half of whatever reward the Emperor bestows upon you today!'

Mahesh Das agreed and bowed before Akbar in the grand Diwan-i-Khas. Akbar recognized the clever young man at once and said, 'Ask for whatever your heart desires, and it shall be granted!'

To the astonishment of the courtiers, Mahesh Das answered, 'Your Majesty, grant me one hundred lashes with a leather whip upon my bare back!'

Akbar was stunned, but keeping his imperial word, he ordered the punishment to begin. After fifty gentle lashes were struck upon a cushioned doublet, Mahesh Das raised his hand: 'Hold, Sire! I have a partner who made me promise to surrender half of my reward before entering your gates.'

He summoned the terrified gatekeeper. When Akbar learned of the extortion, he ordered the remaining fifty fierce lashes administered to the greedy guard, banishing him from service. Impressed by Mahesh Das's brilliance and sense of justice, Akbar appointed him chief counselor, giving him the title Birbal.

title: The Crows in the Kingdom
full_text:
On a breezy summer morning, Emperor Akbar stood with Birbal upon the marble terrace of the Agra Fort, gazing out over the sprawling city, the glittering Yamuna, and the flock of crows wheeling in the pale sky. In a playful mood, the Emperor decided to test his courtiers' wits with an impossible puzzle.

Turning to his assembled ministers, Akbar commanded, 'Tell me at once—how many crows reside within the borders of my capital city of Agra? I want an exact count by sunset, or each of you shall forfeit a week's allowance!'

The courtiers looked at one another in sheer terror. Counting crows was madness! They flitted from rooftop to minaret, roosted in trees, and flew across riverbanks without pause. While the other nobles whispered anxiously and wrung their hands, Birbal stood quietly, smiling with gentle amusement.

'Well, Birbal,' Akbar demanded, 'do you know the answer, or does your wisdom fail before common birds?'

Birbal bowed low with folded hands. 'Sire, the count is simple. There are exactly fifty-two thousand, four hundred and sixty-three crows in the city of Agra.'

Akbar raised his eyebrows in astonishment. 'Are you certain of this figure, Birbal? What if my royal inspectors count them and find a different number?'

'Your Majesty,' Birbal replied without a heartbeat's hesitation, 'if your guards find more crows than my number, it simply means their relatives from neighboring kingdoms have come to visit them in Agra for the summer holidays. And if they find fewer, it means that some of our Agra crows have flown away to visit their cousins in Delhi or Lahore!'

A burst of hearty laughter broke from Emperor Akbar's chest. Delighted by Birbal's unassailable presence of mind, he rewarded him with a string of lustrous pearls, remarking that wit can illuminate even the most absurd corners of life.

title: How Many Crows?
full_text:
Following Birbal's famous answer regarding the crows of Agra, an arrogant nobleman from Kashmir arrived at the imperial court. Jealous of Birbal's towering reputation, the nobleman sneered before Emperor Akbar: 'Your Majesty, it is easy to give a fanciful number when one knows nobody can verify it. Birbal merely invented fifty-two thousand crows out of thin air. A true counselor speaks only of what can be proven!'

Akbar looked at Birbal with twinkling eyes. 'Birbal, our esteemed guest disputes your calculation. How do you defend your honor?'

Birbal remained calm and unruffled. He bowed toward the visiting nobleman and said with polite warmth: 'My lord speaks with admirable caution. Truth is indeed sacred. Therefore, I propose a fair trial. The nobleman himself shall lead three hundred imperial scribes into the streets of Agra tomorrow at dawn to count every crow.'

'Gladly!' the nobleman proclaimed. 'I shall prove your claim false before dusk!'

'However,' Birbal added gently, 'as a man of strict proof, my lord must ensure two conditions. First, while counting, he must confirm that no mother crow lays an egg that hatches during the day, for a newly hatched chick would alter the count. Second, he must certify that no crow perishes from old age or flies across the city gate to peck at grain outside the walls during the census.'

The Kashmiri nobleman stood frozen. 'How can any mortal control when a wild bird hatches, flies, or dies?'

'Precisely,' Birbal answered softly. 'When a man demands absolute certainty regarding matters subject to perpetual change, he chases smoke with a sieve. Wisdom lies in recognizing the difference between meaningful knowledge and pointless wrangling.'

The Emperor nodded in agreement and the nobleman, thoroughly humbled, offered Birbal his sincere respect. Akbar commended his minister for showing that true intelligence disarms pompous doubt with effortless grace.

title: The Cook's Pot
full_text:
The head chef of the imperial palace kitchens rushed into the Diwan-i-Am, trembling with dread. An heirloom cooking vessel—an exquisitely carved silver pot encrusted with turquoise beads, used solely to prepare saffron mutton for state banquets—had vanished from the pantry during the midnight watch.

Emperor Akbar was furious. 'Ten guards and six under-cooks were on duty! Line them up immediately! If the thief does not confess, all sixteen shall be imprisoned!'

Birbal stepped forward. 'Sire, allow me to inspect the scene. An innocent man should not suffer for a thief's misdeed.'

Birbal had all sixteen kitchen staff brought into a private courtyard. In the center stood an ordinary iron cauldron covered with thick black soot from the hearths. Birbal addressed the men solemnly: 'Inside this cauldron resides a magical djinn gifted by an Arabian sage. Each of you must step forward, close your eyes, reach into the cauldron, and firmly press the bottom. When an innocent man touches it, the djinn remains silent. But when the thief presses it, the djinn will utter a thunderous screech!'

One by one, the servants and guards stepped forward, placed their hands deep inside the pot, and stepped back. Not a sound was heard.

The head chef cried, 'The djinn stayed silent! Does this mean the thief escaped?'

'Not at all,' Birbal smiled. 'Please ask every man to open his palms and hold them toward the sky.'

Fifteen men displayed palms covered in thick, greasy black soot. But the third assistant cook held out hands that were spotless and clean!

'Here is your thief,' Birbal announced. 'The innocent men trusted the truth and pressed the pot firmly, getting their hands black with soot. But the thief, terrified that the magic pot would scream, hovered his fingers in the air without touching the bottom!'

Caught red-handed by his own fear, the trembling cook fell to his knees, confessed where he had buried the silver pot, and begged for mercy. Akbar praised Birbal's brilliant psychological deduction.

title: The Brahmin's Dream
full_text:
In the bustling market of Agra lived a wealthy and ruthless moneylender named Seth Girdhari. One night, an honest but impoverished Brahmin scholar named Harishchandra fell into a fitful slumber and dreamed that he approached Girdhari's shop and borrowed one hundred gold mohurs to pay for his daughter's wedding.

The next morning, the guileless scholar met his neighbors near the well and innocently shared his dream: 'Ah, if only dreams were true! Last night I dreamed Seth Girdhari lent me a hundred gold coins without hesitation!'

Word reached the greedy moneylender's ears. Crafty and devoid of conscience, Girdhari immediately marched to the scholar's humble cottage with two burly bailiffs, demanding: 'Repay the hundred gold mohurs you borrowed from me last night, plus ten coins of interest!'

'Are you mad?' the scholar cried. 'It was only a dream!'

'A loan acknowledged before witnesses is a binding debt!' Girdhari sneered, dragging the weeping scholar before Emperor Akbar's imperial throne.

Akbar was perplexed by the bizarre dispute. Sensing an extortionate trick, he turned to Birbal. 'Can a man be compelled to pay for what transpired in a dream?'

Birbal smiled pleasantly. 'Certainly, Your Majesty. A dream debt must be settled with absolute punctuality.'

Birbal instructed an attendant to bring a heavy wooden chest containing one hundred gleaming gold mohurs and place it on a low table. Next, he ordered a large, crystal-clear mirror brought and stood behind the open chest.

The moneylender's eyes bulged with greed as he reached for the gold.

'Halt!' Birbal commanded. 'Do not touch the real gold, Seth Girdhari. The scholar borrowed gold in a dream, which is merely a reflection of the mind. Therefore, you are entitled to take every single gold coin you see reflected inside the mirror!'

The courtiers burst into cheers while Girdhari turned pale with embarrassment. Shamed before the Emperor, the moneylender fled the court, and the poor scholar was blessed with royal protection.

title: The Question of Heirs
full_text:
A wealthy merchant of Delhi passed away, leaving behind three sons and a secret brass casket filled with flawless rubies. Because the merchant had been bedridden for years, rumors abounded that two of the sons were adopted foundlings, while only one was his biological flesh and blood. The merchant's cryptic will stated: 'Let my true son possess the casket of gems; let the others receive five silver dinars each.'

Unable to agree on who was the rightful heir, the three brothers traveled to Agra and pleaded before Emperor Akbar. Each brother claimed: 'I am the eldest and most devoted son! The rubies belong to me!'

Akbar was baffled. There were no birth certificates or family elders left alive to testify. He entrusted the matter to Birbal.

The next morning, Birbal had an artist paint an extraordinarily lifelike portrait of the late merchant. Birbal mounted the portrait on a wooden post at the far end of the garden pavilion, placed a bow and three iron-tipped arrows on a velvet cushion, and addressed the three brothers:

'He who can shoot an arrow directly into the heart of this portrait shall be declared the true, courageous son of the merchant and receive the casket of rubies.'

The eldest brother took the bow without hesitation. He notched an arrow, aimed steadily, and struck the portrait in the left shoulder. 'A near hit!' he boasted.

The second brother stepped forward eagerly. He drew the bowstring to his ear and loosed a shaft that pierced the painted throat. 'I have nearly struck the mark!' he shouted.

Finally, Birbal handed the bow to the youngest brother. The young man held the bow with trembling fingers. Looking at the painted face of the father who had cradled him in childhood, tears flooded his eyes. He dropped the bow and fell to his knees:

'Kill me if you must, but I cannot drive an arrow into the likeness of my beloved father! Keep the rubies, give them to my brothers—I want no treasure purchased with disrespect!'

Birbal lifted the weeping youth and said to Akbar: 'Here is the true son. Greed easily desecrates a father's memory, but genuine filial love cannot wound even his portrait.'

Akbar awarded the entire inheritance to the youngest brother, praising Birbal's profound insight into the human heart.

title: Birbal Identifies the Thief
full_text:
A wealthy diamond merchant named Dhanpat Rai arrived at Emperor Akbar's court in deep distress. 'Your Majesty,' he lamented, 'last night my bedroom chest was unlocked and my heirloom diamond ring, worth twenty thousand rupees, was stolen. No windows were broken, and only my seven personal servants had access to the inner chamber. Yet every single servant swears on his life that he is innocent!'

Akbar summoned the seven servants and questioned them sternly, but all shed tears and denied the crime. Unable to detect the culprit, Akbar called upon Birbal.

'Do not worry, Seth Dhanpat Rai,' Birbal reassured the merchant. 'Guilt cannot hide from the ancient wisdom of the forest.'

Birbal retired to an anteroom and emerged carrying seven slender bamboo rods, each cut to the exact length of twelve inches. He handed one stick to each of the seven suspects and announced:

'These are enchanted bamboo rods obtained from a Himalayan hermit. Tonight, each of you shall keep his stick beneath his sleeping mat. By morning, the stick belonging to the guilty thief will miraculously grow by exactly two inches through mystical power! Tomorrow at sunrise, return here and present your sticks to the Emperor.'

The servants bowed and returned to their quarters. Six of the men, possessing clean consciences, slept soundly throughout the night.

However, the third servant, who had indeed stolen the diamond ring, tossed and turned in terror. 'If my stick grows two inches by sunrise, my guilt will be glaringly obvious! What should I do?'

In the dead of night, he crept into the kitchen, took a sharp knife, and carefully sawed off exactly two inches from his bamboo stick. 'Now,' he thought smugly, 'when it grows two inches tonight, it will match the twelve-inch length of the others, and I shall be safe!'

At dawn, the seven servants lined up before the Emperor. Birbal collected the sticks and measured them with an ivory ruler. Six sticks measured precisely twelve inches. But the thief's stick measured only ten inches!

'Arrest him!' Birbal commanded. 'The sticks were ordinary bamboo with no magic at all. But your guilty conscience shortened what you feared would grow!'

The trembling servant confessed, returned the ring, and the entire court marveled at Birbal's clever trap.

title: The Lost Ring
full_text:
Emperor Akbar was known to possess a magnificent emerald ring, gifted to him by the Shah of Persia. One afternoon, while washing his hands in the imperial dressing room adjacent to the council hall, he slipped the precious ring from his finger and placed it upon a marble pedestal. Upon returning half an hour later, the ring was gone.

Only eight trusted courtiers and personal attendants had been present in the inner chambers during that brief interval. Akbar was heartbroken and enraged: 'One of my own trusted nobles has stolen my ring! If the culprit does not confess, I shall banish all eight from the court forever!'

The courtiers fell upon their faces, swearing loyalty and protesting their innocence. Sensing that an accusation without proof would breed resentment among his closest aides, Akbar turned to Birbal: 'You were not present in the room. Can your intellect uncover which of these eight men has stolen my emerald?'

Birbal observed the eight men carefully. Their faces were masks of righteous indignation, yet he knew that human anxiety always seeks an outlet.

Birbal stepped before the assembly and said in a grave, carrying voice: 'Sire, the emerald ring has not left this chamber. In fact, a supernatural djinn who guards the imperial throne has just whispered the secret into my ear. The djinn revealed that the man who took the ring was careless—a piece of dried straw from the carpet is currently clinging to his beard!'

The words had barely left Birbal's lips when one of the senior courtiers reflexively raised his right hand and nervously patted his beard to brush the invisible straw away!

Birbal immediately pointed at him: 'Seize that man, guards! Search his robes!'

The guards stepped forward, searched the pale courtier's sash, and pulled forth Emperor Akbar's gleaming emerald ring.

'How did you know he had a straw in his beard?' Akbar asked in amazement.

Birbal smiled. 'Your Majesty, there was no straw and no djinn. An innocent man hears such a statement and remains motionless, knowing his beard is clean. Only the guilty man panics and reaches to conceal his guilt!'

Akbar embraced Birbal warmly, marveling at how a master of human nature can solve in a second what brute force cannot untangle in a month.

title: The Farmer's Dispute
full_text:
A hardworking farmer named Ramu saved his hard-earned savings for years to purchase a stone well from his wealthy neighbor, Seth Banwari, to irrigate his parched fields. After signing the sale deed before village elders and paying a handsome sum of gold coins, Ramu walked joyfully to the well the next morning with his bullocks and water buckets.

Just as he lowered his first leather bucket into the cool depths, Banwari marched out of his house and seized the rope: 'Stop, you thief! What do you think you are doing?'

'I am drawing water from my well!' Ramu replied, bewildered.

Banwari grinned maliciously. 'I sold you the stone well, Ramu, but I never sold you the water inside it! The water remains my private property. If you draw even a single drop, you must pay me five silver coins per bucket, or leave the water untouched!'

Heartbroken and ruined, Ramu traveled to Agra, threw himself at Emperor Akbar's feet, and recounted the landlord's deceitful scheme. Akbar was deeply disturbed by the merchant's brazen trickery and asked Birbal to resolve the dispute.

Birbal summoned Banwari to the imperial court. The landlord arrived with his legal scroll, smirking confidently: 'Your Majesty, a contract is sacred in your empire. The deed clearly states I transferred ownership of the stone masonry and soil of the well. It does not mention the water. The water is mine!'

Birbal stroked his chin thoughtfully. 'Your argument is impeccably logical, Seth Banwari. Since you sold the well to Ramu, the physical structure belongs solely to him. And since you did not sell the water, the water belongs solely to you.'

Banwari beamed with triumph. 'Thank you, wise minister!'

'However,' Birbal continued with a sudden, razor-sharp smile, 'since the well belongs entirely to Ramu, you have no right to keep your water inside his property! You are trespassing! You must remove every single drop of your water from Ramu's well before sunset today. And for every hour your water has occupied his well since yesterday, you must pay Ramu a storage fee of one hundred gold mohurs!'

Banwari's jaw dropped. His face turned ashen. To remove thousands of gallons of water within hours was impossible, and the storage fee would bankrupt him!

Realizing his cunning trap had snapped shut upon his own neck, the greedy landlord fell at Ramu's feet, begging for forgiveness and relinquishing all claims to the water forever. Akbar rewarded Ramu and praised Birbal's peerless jurisprudence.

title: Akbar and the Line Drawing
full_text:
During a quiet afternoon in the Diwan-i-Khas, Emperor Akbar sat upon his golden throne in a philosophical mood. Courtiers and scholars surrounded him, each eager to demonstrate superior intellect. Akbar picked up a piece of white chalk from a table, walked to the center of the polished marble floor, and drew a straight white line about two paces long.

Turning to his assembly, Akbar declared: 'Here is my challenge to the wise men of Hindustan. You must make this chalk line shorter. However, you must not touch it, rub it out, erase any part of it, cover it with cloth, or scratch the floor in any way! He who succeeds shall receive a jagir of five fertile villages.'

The ministers hurried forward to inspect the line. One courtier suggested blowing air upon it, but the chalk remained fast. Another suggested pouring water near it, but Akbar forbade touching the floor. A third argued that if one looked at it from across the room, perspective made it seem smaller, but Akbar laughed and rejected the excuse. One by one, the nobles shook their heads and confessed defeat.

'Birbal,' Akbar challenged with a proud smile, 'can even your intellect shorten what cannot be touched?'

Birbal stepped forward with a serene bow. He took another piece of chalk from the Emperor's hand, knelt down beside Akbar's line, and drew a second line parallel to it—making his line twice as long and bold.

Standing up, Birbal gestured to both markings: 'Behold, Your Majesty. I have not touched your line, nor erased a speck of chalk. Yet compared to the new line I have drawn beside it, your line has instantly become shorter!'

The court fell silent for a heartbeat, then erupted into thunderous applause. Akbar smiled warmly and embraced his minister:

'Birbal, you have not merely solved a riddle; you have given us a timeless sermon. In life, petty men seek to diminish others by slander, jealousy, and tearing down their work. But the noble soul diminishes envy simply by expanding his own excellence and doing greater good!'

title: Birbal and the Jealous Courtiers
full_text:
Birbal's towering influence with Emperor Akbar aroused bitter jealousy among several senior courtiers, led by the royal treasurer. Desperate to eliminate him, they bribed the Emperor's personal barber with a sack of gold to execute a ruthless conspiracy.

While trimming Akbar's beard one morning, the barber sighed deeply and said, 'Your Majesty, last night I dreamed of your revered father, Emperor Humayun, residing in the celestial gardens of paradise.'

Akbar, who deeply loved his late father, sat up eagerly: 'What did he say to you?'

'Alas, Sire, he is in divine bliss, yet he feels terribly lonely. He complained that while heaven has poets and musicians, it lacks a companion of brilliant wit like Raja Birbal to entertain him! He asked if you could send Birbal to heaven to keep him company.'

Gullible in matters of family affection, Akbar summoned Birbal and hesitantly explained the request: 'Birbal, my father desires your presence in heaven. Will you make the journey?'

Birbal instantly recognized the conspirators' deadly hand. Going to 'heaven' meant being burned alive on a funeral pyre! Keeping his composure, Birbal bowed: 'It is the supreme honor of my life to serve your noble father, Sire. I ask only for one month's leave to settle my family affairs, and permission to be dispatched from my own ancestral garden.'

Akbar gladly granted the request. During that month, Birbal hired trusted miners to dig a secret underground tunnel from the center of his garden directly into the cellar of his private house, concealing the entrance beneath wooden planks and turf.

On the appointed day, a massive crowd gathered in Birbal's garden. A great pyre of sandalwood and incense was prepared over the hidden trapdoor. Birbal stepped onto the wood, offered prayers, and as thick clouds of smoke billowed upward, he slipped through the secret hatch into the safety of his underground tunnel. The conspirators celebrated, believing Birbal was reduced to ashes.

For six months, Birbal stayed hidden in his home, allowing his hair and beard to grow wild and long.

One bright morning, Birbal walked into Akbar's Diwan-i-Am, clad in silk robes with a magnificent flowing beard. Akbar leaped from his throne: 'Birbal! You have returned from heaven! How is my father?'

'Your father is in radiant health, Sire, and sends his deepest blessings!' Birbal reported. 'He enjoys celestial ambrosia daily. However, heaven has one severe shortage.'

'What is that?' Akbar asked anxiously.

'Sire, there are no barbers in paradise! His Majesty's beard has grown down to his knees, and he urgently commands that you dispatch your own royal barber to heaven without delay!'

The royal barber, standing nearby, turned white as milk. He fell to his knees, confessed the entire conspiracy, and named the jealous courtiers. Akbar banished the wicked nobles and rewarded Birbal for his matchless survival and cunning.

title: The Gold Coins and the Judge
full_text:
Before embarking on a three-year pilgrimage to Mecca, an honest merchant of Agra named Abdullah sealed one hundred gleaming gold dinars inside a sturdy earthenware jar, covered the gold with pickled olives, and entrusted the jar to the city's chief Qazi (judge) for safekeeping.

'Keep this safe in your cellar, noble Qazi,' Abdullah requested. 'If I do not return, distribute the wealth to orphans.'

Two years passed. One evening, the Qazi's wife craved fresh olives. Remembering the pilgrim's jar, the Qazi opened it. Seeing the plump olives, he spooned some out, only to uncover the glittering gold coins beneath! Greed seized the judge's heart. He dumped all the gold into his private strongbox, threw away the moldering old olives, filled the jar with fresh green olives from the market, and resealed it with wax.

When Abdullah returned to Agra, he thanked the Qazi and retrieved his jar. But upon opening it at home, he found only fresh olives—the gold was gone! He rushed to the Qazi, who shouted: 'Ingrate! You gave me a sealed jar of olives and I returned it untouched! Accuse a holy judge and I will have you whipped!'

Weeping, Abdullah brought his petition to Emperor Akbar, who referred the matter to Birbal.

Birbal examined the jar, the seal, and the olives. He summoned two master olive merchants of Agra and asked: 'Examine these olives. How long have they been preserved in this jar?'

The merchants tasted the fruit and replied: 'Sire, these olives are from the recent autumn harvest, barely two months old! Olives kept in a jar for three years would be black, soft, and sour.'

Birbal turned to the Qazi: 'Abdullah departed three years ago. If this jar remained untouched in your cellar as you swear, how did fresh autumn olives find their way into a three-year-old seal?'

The Qazi began to stammer, claiming Abdullah must have replaced them himself.

Birbal then ordered a brazier brought to the chamber. He carefully scraped a speck of sealing wax from the rim and warmed it, comparing it to the official seal currently resting upon the Qazi's desk. The wax was fresh imperial crimson wax, introduced to Agra only six months earlier, whereas three years ago the court used dark brown lac!

Trapped by forensic proof and the testimony of nature, the Qazi broke down and wept, confessing his theft. Akbar stripped the corrupt judge of his office, restored the gold to Abdullah with interest, and lauded Birbal's meticulous discernment.

title: The Boy Who Wanted to Meet Akbar
full_text:
In a small hamlet outside Fatehpur Sikri lived an observant twelve-year-old boy named Mohan, whose greatest ambition was to behold Emperor Akbar with his own eyes. However, ordinary village folk were strictly barred from the imperial red sandstone gates unless summoned for court disputes.

One morning, hearing that Emperor Akbar was inspecting the royal stables near the city walls, Mohan carried a clay bowl filled with fresh wild berries picked from the thorny hills. Approaching the royal perimeter, a fierce guard leveled a spear at his chest: 'Halt, peasant boy! What business do you have near the Shadow of God?'

Mohan bowed politely and said: 'Noble soldier, I bring a gift for the Emperor that no jeweler in Agra can provide.'

Akbar, overhearing the bold declaration from his horse, called the boy over: 'What is this gift, child, that my jewelers cannot match?'

Mohan presented his bowl: 'Sire, wild mountain berries, sweet as nectar, ripened by the sun and washed by morning dew. Your jewelers have diamonds, but they cannot create life or sweetness.'

Pleased by the child's poetic spirit, Akbar tasted a berry and smiled. 'You speak well, boy. But tell me—do you know how to tell a wise man from a fool?'

'Easily, Your Majesty,' Mohan replied without blinking. 'A wise man listens twice as much as he speaks, which is why nature gave us two ears and only one mouth. A fool speaks twice as much as he listens, believing the world hungers for his noise.'

Akbar laughed with joy. Birbal, who was standing beside the Emperor's stallion, nodded with deep admiration: 'Sire, this child possesses the seeds of true discernment.'

Akbar handed Mohan a golden coin and said: 'Go home, clever boy, and study your books with diligence. When you are grown, return to this court, for Hindustan is always in need of minds that see truth with clarity.' Mohan bowed low, clutching his treasure, having proven that intelligence knows no age or poverty.

title: Birbal and the Painter
full_text:
A talented portrait artist of Agra was commissioned by a notoriously stingy merchant named Seth Chhaganlal to paint his portrait for fifty silver rupees. The artist labored for three weeks, capturing every nuance of the merchant's features—his sharp nose, arched eyebrows, and embroidered silk turban.

When the portrait was unveiled, the cunning merchant decided he did not want to part with his silver. He sneered, 'This looks nothing like me! Look at my cheeks—they are fuller than this! Repaint it, or I shall not pay a single dam!'

The patient painter took the canvas back, adjusted the cheeks, and returned. But Chhaganlal had shaved his beard and narrowed his lips, claiming again: 'A terrible failure! The jawline is completely wrong!'

The artist painted three different portraits over two months, but on each visit, the dishonest merchant deliberately changed his facial expression, puffing his cheeks, squinting his eyes, or altering his mustache, refusing to pay. title: The Three Baskets
full_text:
During an evening assembly of philosophers and scholars at Fatehpur Sikri, Emperor Akbar posed a deep metaphysical riddle to his courtiers:

'We speak endlessly of Truth, Illusion, and Falsehood. Can these abstract concepts be captured and held in one's hands? Birbal, I command you: tomorrow morning, bring before my throne three ordinary wicker baskets—one filled with pure Truth, one filled with pure Illusion, and one filled with pure Falsehood!'

The scholars scoffed quietly, convinced that Birbal had finally been trapped by an impossible imperial whim. How could any mortal shovel truth or falsehood into a basket?

The following morning, Birbal walked into the Diwan-i-Khas followed by three palace porters, each carrying a woven wicker basket covered with silk cloth.

Akbar leaned forward with keen curiosity: 'Have you brought what I commanded, Birbal?'

'Yes, Your Majesty,' Birbal answered respectfully.

He removed the cloth from the first basket. It was filled to the brim with coarse white rock salt. 'Sire, this is Truth. Salt is humble, simple, and unadorned. Yet without it, no food on earth has flavor or nourishment. If taken in excess, it bites; if absent, life withers. Truth is raw and unyielding, yet essential for the survival of every soul.'

Next, Birbal uncovered the second basket. Inside rested a polished glass prism and a handful of iridescent peacock feathers that shimmered in colors of emerald, sapphire, and gold depending on the angle of the light. 'Sire, this is Illusion (Maya). From this angle it appears blue, from that angle green, and under shadow it turns dull brown. It dazzles the senses and stirs wonder, yet possesses no permanent reality of its own.'

Finally, Birbal uncovered the third basket. The basket was completely empty, save for a scroll inscribed with courtly panegyrics praising a notoriously cowardly minister as a fearless lion of war.

'And what is this?' Akbar asked.

'Sire, this is Falsehood (Asatya). It promises everything, flatters the vain, and dresses itself in grand words, yet when you reach inside to grasp its substance, you find only empty air and deceit that starves the spirit.'

The assembly broke into spontaneous acclaim. Akbar stood from his throne and embraced Birbal, declaring that wisdom shines brightest when brought down to earth where all can understand.

title: Birbal's Khichdi
full_text:
During a bitterly cold winter in Agra, when frost coated the palace marble and icy winds blew from the northern mountains, Emperor Akbar looked out at the freezing Yamuna river and wondered aloud: 'Can any mortal man endure standing chest-deep in this freezing water from sunset to sunrise for the sake of money?'

A poor, shivering washerman named Dinu stepped forward: 'Your Majesty, my family is starving. If you promise me a reward of two thousand gold coins, I shall stand in the river all night.'

Akbar agreed, posting guards on the riverbank to ensure Dinu did not leave the water. Through the long, agonizing night of howling winds and numbing frost, Dinu stood waist-deep in the black river, fixing his eyes upon a solitary lantern glowing atop the distant palace tower to keep his mind from succumbing to despair. At dawn, trembling violently and barely alive, the brave washerman was brought before Akbar to claim his reward.

Akbar asked: 'How did you survive such freezing torment without dying?'

Dinu replied humbly: 'Sire, whenever the cold threatened to stop my heart, I gazed upon the warm light of your palace lantern glowing far away on the horizon, and the thought of your generosity kept me alive.'

A jealous courtier whispered: 'Sire! He was warmed by your royal lantern! He did not endure the cold unaided; he absorbed heat from your palace!'

Gullible to the courtier's argument, Akbar declared: 'You cheated, Dinu! You warmed yourself with my lantern light! You shall receive no reward.'

Heartbroken, the poor washerman wept and went to Birbal.

The next day, Akbar waited in the Diwan-i-Khas, but Birbal did not appear. When noon passed, Akbar sent an attendant, who reported that Birbal was in his garden cooking khichdi (rice and lentils). By late afternoon, Birbal was still absent. Curious and impatient, Akbar rode to Birbal's house.

In the garden, Akbar found Birbal sitting beside a tiny fire of dry twigs burning on the grass. High above, tied to the branch of a tall tamarind tree nearly twenty feet in the air, hung an iron cooking pot!

Akbar laughed: 'Birbal, have you lost your senses? How can the heat from that tiny fire on the ground reach a pot hanging twenty cubits in the sky? Your khichdi will never cook!'

Birbal looked into Akbar's eyes with solemn dignity: 'Your Majesty, if the gentle heat of a palace lantern two miles away can warm a poor washerman freezing in the icy river Yamuna, then surely this fire can cook my khichdi twenty feet above!'

Akbar froze. The absurdity of his own verdict struck him with the force of a thunderbolt. Ashamed of his cruelty, the Emperor immediately summoned Dinu, presented him with four thousand gold coins and a robe of honor, and thanked Birbal for saving him from the sin of injustice.

title: The Biggest Thing?
full_text:
On a clear night under a canopy of blazing stars, Emperor Akbar and his courtiers stood upon the ramparts of Fatehpur Sikri. Contemplating the vastness of creation, Akbar turned to his ministers and asked:

'What is the biggest, most expansive thing in this universe? Some say it is the boundless ocean; others say it is the soaring sky or the great earth itself. What say you, wise counselors?'

One minister bowed: 'Sire, it is the earth, which bears mountains, empires, and oceans upon its breast.'

Another argued: 'No, it is the sky, for the sky wraps around the entire earth and holds the sun and moon within its mantle.'

A third courtier flattered the monarch: 'Surely, the biggest thing is the imperial heart and fame of Emperor Akbar, which reaches the ends of the world!'

Akbar smiled at the flattery, but turned to his favorite minister: 'Birbal, you remain silent. What is the greatest thing in creation?'

Birbal smiled gently and replied: 'Your Majesty, the biggest thing in the universe is a mother's lap, and beside it, the boundless reach of human imagination.'

The courtiers murmured in surprise. 'A mother's lap? Human imagination? How can those be bigger than the sky?'

Birbal explained with quiet eloquence: 'Sire, consider the sky. It holds the stars, yet it cannot cradle a weeping child, nor comfort a broken spirit. But no matter how tall, powerful, or weary an emperor becomes, when he lays his head upon his mother's lap, the entire world, with all its burdens, fears, and sorrows, shrinks to nothingness within that small circle of tender love. A mother's heart has room for every fault and every sorrow.

'And consider the human mind,' Birbal continued. 'The physical body is trapped in this small courtyard, yet in a single second, human imagination can fly past the farthest star, cross thousands of leagues of ocean, build golden palaces in the clouds, and embrace eternity. Neither earth nor sky can contain what the mind can conceive.'

Tears glistened in Emperor Akbar's eyes as he remembered his own mother, Hamida Banu Begum. He removed a jeweled pendant from his necklace and presented it to Birbal, remarking that true philosophy elevates love and thought above mere physical size.

title: The Wilted Flower
full_text:
In the court of Emperor Akbar, courtiers constantly competed to outdo one another in lavish praise and exaggerated flattery. One sycophantic noble named Mirza Kazim, hoping to win the governorship of a wealthy province, arrived at the morning assembly carrying a magnificent, dew-drenched red rose crafted with such exquisite petals that it looked like a marvel of nature.

Kazim bowed nine times and presented the blossom to Akbar: 'O Shadow of God! So blessed is your imperial reign that even the laws of decay have ceased in my gardens! This rose was plucked seven weeks ago, yet under the radiant aura of your divine justice, it refuses to wither! It remains as fresh as the moment it bloomed!'

Akbar, though wise, was intrigued by the flawless flower. 'Can this be true? Does nature herself halt her cycles in honor of our throne?'

The courtiers chorused in unison: 'Undoubtedly, Sire! The Emperor's virtue preserves all beauty!'

Birbal sat quietly in his pavilion, observing the waxy sheen along the petal edges and the stiff symmetry of the leaves. He stepped forward with a humble bow:

'Sire, Mirza Kazim's devotion is touching. Yet before we record this miracle in the imperial annals, let us consult the most impartial judges in your empire.'

Birbal gestured to an attendant in the palace garden. A moment later, the attendant brought a small bamboo cage containing three live honeybees collected from the jasmine bushes.

Birbal opened the cage door in the center of the hall. The three bees buzzed into the air. They flew past Mirza Kazim's magnificent rose without pausing for a single second, circled the hall, and flew straight out the open arched window to alight upon a tiny, wilting wild marigold growing in a crack between the marble steps outside!

Birbal smiled: 'Behold, Your Majesty. Man can carve wax, paint silk, and scent dead clay with rosewater to flatter an emperor. But the humble bee seeks only life and nectar. It knows that Mirza Kazim's rose is made of painted wax, while the wilting weed outside possesses genuine life created by the Almighty.'

Akbar examined the rose closely, felt the softening wax beneath his warm fingers, and frowned with displeasure at the fawning courtier. Mirza Kazim slunk away in disgrace, while Akbar thanked Birbal for keeping his court grounded in honesty.

title: The Four Fools
full_text:
One afternoon, having listened to endless petty squabbles in the court, Emperor Akbar sighed in exasperation and said to Birbal: 'Our empire seems overflowing with foolishness! Birbal, I give you three days to scour the city of Agra and bring before me the four greatest fools in Hindustan!'

Birbal bowed and departed. For two days he roamed the bazaars, riverbanks, and highways of Agra, observing human behavior with an amused eye.

On the third day, Birbal returned to the Diwan-i-Khas, accompanied by only two men.

The first man was carrying a heavy bundle of dry hay on his own head, even though he was riding on the back of a sturdy donkey!

Akbar looked at the rider in disbelief: 'Man, why are you carrying that heavy bundle of hay upon your own skull instead of placing it on the donkey's back?'

The rider replied with sincere worry: 'Sire, my poor donkey is already carrying my heavy body! If I placed this heavy sack of grass on his back as well, it would crush the poor beast! So I carry it on my own head to lighten his burden!'

Akbar chuckled: 'Truly, this man is a premier fool! And who is the second?'

Birbal pointed to the second man, who was crawling on his hands and knees beneath a brightly lit street lamp in the courtyard, frantically sifting through dust.

Akbar asked: 'What are you searching for, friend?'

The man replied: 'Sire, I lost my gold wedding ring in the dark forest two miles outside the city gate!'

'Then why on earth are you searching for it here in the palace courtyard?' Akbar demanded.

The man replied innocently: 'Because it was pitch black in the forest, Sire, and there is plenty of light here under this palace lamp!'

The court roared with laughter. Akbar turned to Birbal: 'These two are indeed magnificent fools, Birbal. But I commanded you to bring four fools! Where are the other two?'

Birbal folded his hands and looked at Akbar with serene respect:

'Your Majesty, the third fool is myself—who spent three precious days neglecting vital governance and the welfare of the people to hunt down harmless fools!

'And with deepest humility, Sire, the fourth fool is Your Imperial Majesty—who commissioned a wise minister to waste imperial time and treasury on such a nonsensical quest instead of attending to the affairs of state!'

The courtiers gasped in horror at Birbal's astonishing audacity. But Akbar stared at Birbal for a tense moment, then threw his head back and laughed till tears filled his eyes:

'You speak the absolute truth, Birbal! He who hunts for fools is the greatest fool of all!' Akbar rewarded Birbal with a purse of gold for his fearless honesty.

title: The Mango Thief
full_text:
In a fertile village bordering the river Yamuna, an ancient and extraordinarily sweet mango tree stood near a boundary hedge. That summer, the tree was bowed low with hundreds of golden, fragrant Dussehri mangoes. Two neighboring farmers, Ramlal and Shyamlal, appeared before Emperor Akbar's imperial court, violently shouting and accusing each other.

Ramlal wept: 'Sire! Twelve years ago, I planted the sapling, carried water from the river every morning, fenced it from wild deer, and fertilized the soil! Now that it bears heavenly fruit, Shyamlal claims it grew on his side of the hedge!'

Shyamlal yelled back: 'Lies, Your Majesty! The roots spring from my land! Ramlal is an envious scoundrel who wishes to rob my harvest!'

There were no written land records for the village border, and the village panchayat was evenly divided, half supporting Ramlal and half supporting Shyamlal.

Akbar turned the case over to Birbal. 'How will you uncover who planted the tree twelve years ago?'

Birbal listened to both men, stroked his beard, and said in a grave voice: 'Since the boundary is uncertain and the testimony is deadlocked, neither of you can be granted the tree. The imperial court shall settle this fairly: guards, take axes to the orchard! Chop the mango tree down the middle! Cut the trunk into two equal halves of timber for each man, and divide the plucked mangoes into two equal baskets!'

Shyamlal immediately nodded with enthusiasm: 'A wise and fair judgment! If I cannot have the whole tree, neither shall he! Cut it down at once, Sire!'

Hearing this, Ramlal fell face-down upon the marble floor, weeping piteously:

'No, Emperor! I beg of you, do not chop down the tree! I watered it for twelve long years; it is like my own child! Give the tree and all its sweet mangoes to Shyamlal! Let him have everything, but spare the life of the tree!'

Birbal stepped down from the dais, helped Ramlal to his feet, and addressed Emperor Akbar:

'Your Majesty, the judgment is clear. A thief and an imposter is eager to destroy what he never labored to create, for he cares only for selfish spite. But the true father who nurtured the tree with his sweat would rather surrender his claim than see the living tree slain.'

Akbar awarded the entire orchard to Ramlal, ordered Shyamlal heavily fined and sentenced to prison, and praised Birbal's profound understanding of human devotion.

title: The Cost of a Dream
full_text:
In the bustling Sarafa bazaar of Agra lived a wealthy goldsmith named Moti Lal, infamous across the province for his stinginess. He never gave a copper coin to charity and counted his gold mohurs three times before sleeping.

One evening, an honest weaver named Kalu, exhausted after twelve hours at the loom, had a vivid dream. In his slumber, Kalu dreamed that Moti Lal visited his humble hut, handed him fifty sparkling gold coins, and said: 'Take this loan, Kalu, and buy fine silk thread from Surat.'

The next morning, Kalu jokingly shared the dream with his fellow weavers at the tea stall: 'Can you believe it? In my dream last night, even stingy Moti Lal became a generous moneylender and gave me fifty gold coins!'

Unfortunately, Moti Lal's nephew was sitting nearby. He hurried home and informed his miserly uncle.

Moti Lal's eyes gleamed with twisted greed. 'A public acknowledgment of a loan! The law recognizes oral testimony!'

Accompanied by two muscular debt collectors, Moti Lal marched to the weaver's cottage, demanding: 'Pay me fifty gold mohurs plus ten coins interest for the loan you took last night!'

'Are you out of your mind?' Kalu cried in anguish. 'It was only a dream! I never received a single copper!'

'You confessed before three witnesses at the tea stall!' Moti Lal shouted, dragging the weeping weaver before the imperial court.

Emperor Akbar was appalled by the goldsmith's absurd claim, yet Moti Lal quoted legal codes on public confessions. Akbar looked at Birbal with an exasperated sigh: 'Birbal, can this madness be resolved legally?'

'With absolute precision, Your Majesty,' Birbal replied smoothly.

Birbal ordered a heavy velvet purse containing fifty gold coins brought from the treasury, along with a large, polished brass mirror. Birbal placed the open purse of gold in front of the mirror, so that the coins glittered brightly in the glass.

Birbal said to Moti Lal: 'Sethji, Kalu borrowed gold in a dream. A dream is a shadow of reality, just as a reflection is a shadow of an object. Step forward and collect every single gold coin you see inside the mirror!'

Moti Lal reached forward, only for his fingers to knock against the cold, flat surface of the glass. 'How can I take reflected coins?' he protested.

'Just as Kalu spent dream coins!' Birbal retorted, his eyes flashing. 'If dream money can create a real debt, reflected money can pay it!'

The court erupted in laughter. Akbar fined Moti Lal fifty gold coins for wasting the court's time and awarded the sum to the poor weaver.

title: The Stolen Pearl
full_text:
Emperor Akbar's private jewel master was arranging a tray of nine flawless Persian pearls in the Sheesh Mahal (Palace of Mirrors) when the Emperor summoned him to the balcony. Leaving the velvet tray on a marble table for barely three minutes, the jeweler returned to find the largest pearl—a gem the size of a pigeon's egg, worth a king's ransom—missing from its satin groove.

Only six palace chamberlains had been present in the hallway outside the room. All were trusted men from noble families. When interrogated, all six swore solemn oaths of innocence, tearing their robes in distress.

Akbar summoned Birbal: 'This pearl was an imperial treasure. Yet I cannot torture six noble youths without proof. How can we determine the guilty one?'

Birbal requested that all six chamberlains be brought into a quiet, darkened room lined with mirrors. He placed a bronze bowl filled with pure spring water upon a low table and addressed the men:

'In this holy water, I have dissolved an ancient herbal potion brought from Tibet. It has no smell, but when an innocent man looks into the water, his reflection appears calm and clear. However, when the man who holds the stolen pearl looks into the bowl, the water will instantly reveal a dark shadow over his brow, marking him for the executioner.'

Birbal instructed each man to walk alone to the table, look directly into the water, and return to his place.

Five of the chamberlains walked forward with steady, confident strides, leaned over the bowl, looked deeply into the water, and smiled in relief at their clear reflections.

However, the fourth chamberlain approached with trembling knees. His eyes darted nervously between the water and the ceiling. Terrified that the magic water would reveal his crime, he stepped to the table, squeezed his eyes tightly shut, held his breath, and backed away without looking into the water at all!

Birbal immediately grabbed the fourth chamberlain's wrist: 'Here is your thief, Your Majesty!'

'How can you know?' Akbar asked.

'Sire, the water is ordinary well water. Five innocent men looked into it without fear. But this man was so terrified of what the water might reveal that he closed his eyes tightly, refusing to look at his own reflection!'

The trembling youth fell to his knees, broke down in tears, and pulled the giant pearl from the hollow heel of his leather riding boot. Akbar praised Birbal's psychological genius, which extracted the truth without spilling a single drop of blood.

'Let us test the truth tomorrow, Your Majesty,' Birbal suggested.

title: The Price of Buttermilk
full_text:
In a village along the road to Delhi lived an unscrupulous milkman named Ganga Ram. Every morning, before filling his brass canisters to sell buttermilk to travelers and pilgrims, Ganga Ram stopped at the canal and added an equal amount of dirty river water to the churned buttermilk, doubling his volume and tripling his profit.

When customers complained that the buttermilk tasted watery, Ganga Ram swore on his ancestors: 'I swear by the holy river that this buttermilk is as pure as morning dew!'

Over five years of deceit, Ganga Ram accumulated a heavy leather bag filled with five hundred silver rupees. Smug and wealthy, he decided to travel to the grand festival in Agra to buy gold jewelry for his wife.

On his journey, the afternoon sun beat down with scorching fury. Tired and sweating, Ganga Ram stopped under a sprawling banyan tree beside a deep, clear river. He placed his precious moneybag on a flat rock, took off his clothes, and jumped into the cool water to bathe.

High up in the banyan branches sat a troop of mischievous monkeys. The alpha monkey, seeing the shiny leather bag, scrambled down the trunk, snatched the bag, and leaped to the topmost branch!

Ganga Ram splashed out of the water, screaming in terror: 'Drop that bag, you cursed ape! That is my life's fortune!'

He hurled stones and fruit at the monkey, but the animal only chattered angrily. The monkey untied the leather drawstring, reached inside, and pulled out a handful of silver coins.

Looking down at the frantic milkman, the monkey dropped one silver coin onto the dry grass where Ganga Ram stood. Then, swinging to the outer branch, the monkey dropped the next silver coin into the deep river water! *Plop!*

The monkey continued methodically: one coin dropped to the earth, one coin thrown into the river. One for the land, one for the water.

Ganga Ram wept and tore his hair as two hundred and fifty silver coins sank forever to the muddy river bottom, while two hundred and fifty coins fell upon the riverbank. When the bag was empty, the monkey tossed the leather pouch and bounded away.

Gathering the remaining coins, Ganga Ram sat weeping on the bank. Just then, Birbal, who was traveling back to Agra with a small escort, stopped his horse and inquired about the tragedy.

Hearing the milkman's confession, Birbal smiled with profound irony:

'Do not weep, Ganga Ram. Nature has settled your accounts with perfect mathematics. The money you earned from honest buttermilk fell safely upon the earth for you to keep. The money you earned by watering down milk with river water has returned directly to the river! Divine justice has merely separated the milk from the water.'

Humbled and repentant, Ganga Ram vowed never to dilute his milk again.

title: The Two Men and the Tree
full_text:
Two travelers, Mohan and Sohan, who had known each other since childhood, journeyed together across the dry plains of Malwa. Outside a lonely village, they rested in the shade of a colossal, centuries-old banyan tree. While resting, Sohan fell ill and ran out of money. Taking pity on his friend, Mohan opened his purse and lent Sohan one hundred silver coins, saying: 'Repay me when we return to Agra.'

Sohan wept with gratitude under the tree, swearing: 'May this holy banyan tree be my witness! I shall repay every silver coin the day I return.'

A year later, both men returned to Agra. When Mohan approached Sohan's prosperous house and politely asked for his money, Sohan looked at him with icy disdain: 'What money? I never borrowed a single dam from you! Do you have a written receipt? Do you have witnesses? Get off my porch before I call the guards!'

Heartbroken by the betrayal of friendship, Mohan brought his case before Emperor Akbar's court. Akbar questioned Sohan, who swore with an innocent face: 'Sire, I swear on my sacred honor, Mohan never lent me money. He is inventing stories to extort me.'

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'There are no written documents and no human witnesses. How can this be decided?'

Birbal turned to Mohan: 'Where did you give him the money?'

'Sire, under a colossal, twisted banyan tree ten miles outside the city walls, near the old stone bridge.'

Birbal handed Mohan his royal staff: 'Take this staff, ride to that banyan tree, and say: "Raja Birbal summons you to the imperial court of Emperor Akbar to testify as a witness in this dispute!" Go at once, and we shall await the tree's reply.'

Mohan bowed and departed on a horse.

Birbal instructed Sohan to sit quietly on the floor of the court and wait. An hour passed in absolute silence. The sun climbed higher. Courtiers whispered, amused that Birbal had summoned a tree.

Suddenly, Birbal turned to Sohan and asked casually: 'Sohan, do you think Mohan has reached the banyan tree yet?'

Without thinking, Sohan replied smugly: 'Certainly not, Your Majesty! That banyan tree is more than ten miles away across rough terrain! It will take him at least two more hours to get there!'

Birbal's eyes flashed like lightning. He struck his fist upon the table:

'Caught by your own tongue, scoundrel! If Mohan never lent you money under that banyan tree, and you were never there with him, how did you know the exact distance and location of the tree so accurately?'

Sohan turned pale as death. He fell face-down upon the marble floor, trembling with terror: 'Mercy, Sire! I confessed! I remembered the tree! I will pay Mohan his hundred silver coins immediately!'

When Mohan returned hours later, exhausted, Akbar had already ordered the money recovered with a heavy penalty, praising Birbal for turning an ancient tree into an undeniable witness of truth.

title: The Pot of Buttermilk
full_text:
One balmy evening in Agra, Emperor Akbar was discussing civic duty and public integrity with his ministers. The royal treasurer boasted that the citizens of the capital were so fiercely loyal and devout that every man would gladly sacrifice his finest possessions for the crown.

Birbal smiled gently: 'Sire, people are generous in words when the sun shines, but when self-interest can hide in the dark, human nature often chooses convenience over duty.'

Akbar decided to test his people. He had an enormous marble cistern built in the center of the royal gardens. An imperial proclamation was announced across Agra:

'By imperial decree, every household in Agra must send one representative tonight between midnight and dawn to pour exactly one brass cup of fresh, pure cow's milk into the royal cistern. No one may look inside the pool while pouring, for it is an offering of selfless loyalty!'

Throughout the night, thousands of citizens filed into the moonlit gardens, stepped to the stone rim of the dark reservoir, tipped their vessels, and hurried away.

Every citizen reasoned identically to himself: 'There are fifty thousand families in Agra pouring rich milk into this giant pool. If I pour one cup of plain water instead of milk, no one will notice in the dark, and my cup will be swallowed up by the ocean of white milk!'

At sunrise, Emperor Akbar walked joyfully to the garden with Birbal, expecting to see a fragrant lake of rich, foaming white milk.

Instead, Akbar gasped in disbelief. The cistern was filled to the brim with crystal-clear, transparent water! Not a single citizen had brought milk; every single person had brought water, believing everyone else would supply the milk!

Birbal smiled: 'Behold, Your Majesty. When responsibility is diffused and darkness hides individual actions, men easily shirk their duty, assuming others will carry the burden. True character is what a man does when he believes no one is watching.'

Akbar laughed heartily at the revelation, took the lesson to heart, and commended Birbal for teaching him practical governance.

title: The Farmer's Well and Neighbour
full_text:
In the dry district of Mathura, a hardworking peasant named Haria purchased a deep stone well from a cunning landowner named Seth Jagdish. Haria paid thirty silver rupees before the village council, received the deed, and rejoiced that his wheat fields would finally have water.

However, the very next morning when Haria lowered his rope and leather bucket, Jagdish came running with a thick bamboo cane: 'Hands off! What do you think you are touching, peasant?'

Haria stammered: 'The well, master! I bought it from you yesterday!'

Jagdish sneered arrogantly: 'You bought the stone masonry and the pit in the ground, fool! You did not buy the water that fills it! The water was put there by heaven and remains my private property. If you want my water, pay me two copper coins per bucket, or watch your crops turn to dust!'

Unable to fight the wealthy landowner alone, Haria walked three days to Agra and poured out his sorrow before Emperor Akbar. Akbar was appalled by such shameless trickery. He summoned Jagdish to the Diwan-i-Am.

Jagdish presented the parchment deed, smirking: 'Your Majesty, the law is clear. A contract transfers only what is explicitly written. The word "water" is nowhere on this parchment. The water is mine!'

Akbar turned to Birbal with raised eyebrows. Birbal stood up, bowed politely to the merchant, and said in a calm, melodic voice:

'Seth Jagdish, your legal precision is commendable. You are entirely correct: the deed proves Haria bought only the well, and the water belongs exclusively to you.'

Jagdish bowed proudly: 'Thank you, wise minister!'

'However,' Birbal continued, his eyes sparkling with dangerous brilliance, 'since the well belongs entirely to Haria, you have kept thousands of gallons of your private water stored inside Haria's property without his permission! You are trespassing!

'Therefore, the court orders: you must remove every single drop of your water from Haria's well immediately, without spilling a drop upon his stones! And for every day your water has occupied Haria's well since the sale, you shall pay Haria fifty silver coins in storage rent!'

Jagdish went pale. Remove thousands of tons of water immediately? Pay fifty silver coins a day? The verdict spelled his financial ruin!

Jagdish threw himself into the dust, begged for mercy, and surrendered all claims to the water, granting Haria free use forever. Akbar roared with laughter and praised Birbal's incomparable wit.

title: The King and the Barber
full_text:
The royal barber, Karim, had cut Emperor Akbar's hair and massaged his head with scented almond oil for twelve years. Because the Emperor often made casual conversation during his morning grooming, the barber grew absurdly proud, convincing himself that he understood statecraft far better than the imperial ministers.

One morning, while trimming Akbar's sideburns, Karim remarked: 'Your Majesty, courtiers like Raja Birbal do nothing but talk and make clever jokes, yet they enjoy vast estates! If you gave an ordinary, practical man of the people—such as myself—the position of minister for just one week, I would solve the empire's greatest dilemmas!'

Akbar was amused, but decided to consult Birbal.

When Birbal heard of the barber's ambition, he smiled: 'Sire, let us fulfill his dream tomorrow. Appoint Karim acting minister of the royal stables for one single day.'

Akbar agreed. The next morning, Karim was dressed in embroidered silk robes, given a jeweled turban, and seated in the ministerial pavilion at the royal stables. He puffed out his chest, feeling immensely powerful.

Soon, two burly cavalry officers arrived with two identical white stallions. The officers shouted: 'Minister! These two Arabian stallions were purchased yesterday from a Persian merchant for ten thousand gold mohurs. They look identical, run with identical speed, and have identical markings. But one is four years old, and the other is five years old! We must record their exact ages in the imperial register before noon, or the army treasury will be penalized! Tell us which horse is which!'

Karim stepped forward, sweating in his heavy silk coat. He inspected the horses' ears, stroked their manes, and measured their tails. They looked completely identical! He had no idea what to do. Hours ticked away; the cavalry officers grew impatient and began banging their swords against their shields. The barber began to panic, weeping into his silk sleeves.

Just then, Birbal walked into the stables. Seeing the trembling barber, Birbal asked the grooms to bring a basket of fresh, crunchy sugarcane stalks.

Birbal offered a thick stalk to the first stallion, and another to the second. Both horses munched eagerly. Birbal stepped forward, gently parted their lips, and inspected their teeth:

'Behold,' Birbal showed the officers. 'This stallion has already lost and replaced his corner incisors, which occurs only in a horse's fifth year. This stallion still retains his fourth-year milk corners! The five-year-old is on the right; the four-year-old is on the left.'

The officers cheered and recorded the entries. Karim fell at Birbal's feet, tearing off his ministerial turban: 'Take it back, my lord! I know how to trim hair, but I know nothing of horses or statecraft!'

Birbal helped the humbled barber up, advising him that every honest trade has its honor, but pretending to possess wisdom one has never cultivated leads only to shame.

title: Birbal and the Washerman
full_text:
One morning, Emperor Akbar awoke earlier than usual and walked to his bedroom window overlooking the Yamuna riverbank. The very first person he laid his eyes upon was an old, humpbacked washerman carrying a heavy bundle of laundry.

That day was a catalog of royal disasters. While stepping down the marble terrace, Akbar stubbed his toe painfully. At breakfast, a bee stung his thumb, and hot tea spilled over his silk robes. During the afternoon hunt, his favorite stallion slipped in the mud, throwing the Emperor into a briar patch. By evening, Akbar had developed a pounding headache and received news of a minor border rebellion.

Nursing his bruised forehead, Akbar seethed: 'It was that wretched humpbacked washerman! I saw his unlucky face the moment I opened my eyes! His ill-omened countenance has brought me nothing but agony and misfortune! Guards, arrest that washerman and hang him at the city gates tomorrow at dawn!'

The poor washerman was seized, thrown into the dungeon, and his family wept outside the palace in terror. The washerman managed to send an urgent plea to Birbal.

The next morning, just as the executioner prepared the noose in the courtyard, Birbal arrived with Emperor Akbar.

Birbal stepped before the throne and said: 'Sire, before this man hangs, he has one final question for the Emperor.'

Akbar frowned: 'Let him ask.'

Birbal asked: 'Washerman, who was the very first person you saw when you stepped out of your hut yesterday morning?'

The trembling washerman replied: 'My lord, as I picked up my bundle of laundry, I looked up at the palace terrace and saw the radiant face of our Emperor Akbar!'

Birbal turned to Akbar with profound solemnity:

'Consider this carefully, Your Imperial Majesty. Yesterday morning, you saw the washerman's face, and you merely stubbed your toe, spilled tea, and lost your temper.

'But this poor washerman looked upon Your Majesty's face, and as a direct result, he has lost his liberty, been thrown into chains, and is now about to lose his life on the gallows! Now tell me, Sire—whose face is truly the more unlucky of the two?'

Akbar stood frozen. The mirror of Birbal's logic held up his own superstition and cruelty for the entire court to see. Ashamed of his irrational anger, Akbar ordered the washerman released immediately, gifted him a purse of gold and a house near the river, and vowed never to let superstition guide royal justice again.

title: The Rich Merchant and His Sons
full_text:
A wealthy silk merchant of Agra named Seth Dhaniram approached Emperor Akbar with an unusual petition. Feeling his health failing, Dhaniram explained:

'Your Majesty, I have amassed a fortune of three hundred thousand gold mohurs. I have three grown sons, but I do not know which one possesses the wisdom to preserve my family name. If I divide the fortune equally, a foolish son will squander his share on gambling and bring ruin to all. I beg your royal court to test my sons and name the rightful custodian.'

Akbar turned to Birbal, who agreed to conduct a test.

Birbal summoned the three young men to the palace courtyard. He handed each brother an identical single copper dam (the smallest coin in the empire) and said:

'Here is your trial. Each of you must take this single copper coin to the bazaar. You must buy something with it that will completely fill this entire empty banquet hall from wall to wall and floor to ceiling before sunset. He who succeeds shall inherit his father's entire estate.'

The eldest son hurried to the bazaar, laughing: 'A single copper coin to fill a palace hall? It is impossible! But let me buy the cheapest bulk goods available.' He bought five cartloads of foul-smelling straw and dumped it in the hall. The straw filled only a corner, creating a dusty, sneezing mess.

The second son shook his head: 'Straw is too expensive.' He went to the riverbanks, bought three cartloads of dry autumn leaves, and dumped them inside. The leaves filled only half the floor, blowing everywhere when the wind blew through the archways.

Finally, the youngest son arrived just as the sun dipped beneath the horizon. He carried nothing but a small clay oil lamp and a single sweet-smelling stick of incense, which he had bought for his copper coin.

He placed the lamp in the center of the dark, cavernous hall and struck a flint. Instantly, radiant golden light filled every square inch of the hall, banishing the darkness from wall to wall and ceiling to floor, while the fragrant smoke of the incense filled the air with sweetness!

Birbal smiled proudly: 'Behold, Your Majesty. Folly fills a house with dust and clutter. But wisdom, like light and virtue, requires very little material wealth to illuminate an entire home and bless all who dwell within.'

Akbar and Dhaniram joyfully declared the youngest son the chief heir, teaching the older brothers that intellect is greater than brute accumulation.
